Abstract—The authors report a 71-year-old woman with amphiphysin-associated paraneoplastic stiff-person syndrome,
opsoclonus, and encephalopathy. The patient’s symptoms temporarily responded to plasmapheresis in parallel with a
decline of serum anti-amphiphysin antibody titers. Later, the encephalopathy progressed rapidly and the patient died.
Binding studies and the detection of autoantibodies in the patient’s CNS as well as the treatment response suggest a
pathogenic role of the anti-amphiphysin antibodies.
NEUROLOGY 2003;61:195–198
Stiff-person syndrome occurs as an idiopathic or
paraneoplastic condition and may be associated with
antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) or
the 128 kD synaptic protein amphiphysin.
1 Some pa-
tients with anti-GAD antibodies may respond to
plasmapheresis or immunosuppression.
2,3 We report
a 71-year-old woman with breast cancer with an ul-
timately fatal anti-amphiphysin-associated stiff-
person syndrome, encephalopathy, and opsoclonus.
The response to plasma exchange and the immuno-
pathologic findings suggest a pathogenic role of
autoantibodies.

Case report. A 71-year-old woman developed stiffness in the
right arm, stiff and unsteady gait, and increased sweating. Muscle
tone in the right arm and trunk erectors was markedly increased
and further enhanced by sensory stimuli. CSF showed 6 cells/ /H9262L,
increased protein (117 mg/dL), and identical oligoclonal bands to
serum. Cranial T2-weighted MRI showed slight hyperintensity in
the mediobasal temporal lobes and in the hypothalamus. Diaze-
pam treatment induced a marked but short-lasting improvement.
Despite additional treatment with baclofen and high-dose ste-
roids, the patient deteriorated within 4 weeks with increased tone
in the left arm and in the legs, inability to walk or stand, memory
impairment, disorientation, and opsoclonus. Mammography
showed microcalcifications in the right breast. The breast and
lymph nodes were removed and an invasive-ductal carcinoma with
axillary lymph node metastases was diagnosed. Anti-GAD, anti-
Yo, and anti-Hu antibodies were negative, but high titer anti-
amphiphysin antibodies were detected in the patient’s serum and
CSF (Dr. Seelig, Karlsruhe, Germany). Plasma exchange treat-
ment (PE) was initiated 10 weeks after the first symptoms had
started. During a series of 11 PE, the increased muscle tone was
normalized, and the patient was able to walk again with help,
associated with a 16-fold drop of the serum anti-amphiphysin
antibody titers (1:3,280,000 to 1:205,000; figure 1a). Under treat-
ment with cyclophosphamide (3 /H11003350 mg/m
2, monthly doses of
600 mg/m 2 IV), the patient’s mental state and opsoclonus im-
proved over 3 months; titers then were 1:12,800. One month later,
the disease recurred and titers increased (1:205,000). The T2-
weighted MRI now showed marked hyperintense lesions in the
pons (figure 1, b and c). Despite repeated PE and lowering of the
antibody titer, the patient’s condition progressed until death from
pneumonia 8 months after disease onset.
Materials and methods. Brain and spinal cord were removed 4
hours postmortem. Immunohistochemical staining for GFAP,
CD8, CD20, CD68, C5b9 (DAKO, Hamburg, Germany), CD3, and
CD4 (Novocastra, Newcastle, UK) was carried out on 4-/H9262m-thick

paraffin sections applying the avidin-biotin-complex (ABC) perox-
idase method (Merck, Darmstadt, Germany). Immunofluorescent
double labeling was performed on 10-/H9262m frozen sections.
Binding studies were performed with plasma filtrate from the
patient, from an anti-GAD-positive patient with stiff-person syn-
drome, from an age-matched patient with hyperviscosity syn-
drome, and with serum from three healthy controls. Dilutions of
1:100 to 1:50,000 were used overnight as primary antibodies on
sections from the pons and spinal cord of the patient, from a
control autopsy, and from rat cerebellum, brainstem, and spinal
cord. Peroxidase-conjugated rabbit anti-human immunoglobulin G
(IgG) antibodies (DAKO) were used as secondary antibodies at
1:200 for 30 minutes. A similar protocol was followed using com-
mercially available rabbit-anti-human anti-GAD (Chemicon, Hof-
heim, Germany) and anti-amphiphysin antisera (IIM GmbH,
Karlsruhe, Germany) and an ABC-System (Vector, Burlingame,
CA). A competition experiment was performed where the patient’s
plasma filtrate was overlaid on rat spinal cord sections overnight
at 4 °C before immunohistochemistry with anti-amphiphysin anti-
serum was performed. To assess whether endogenous immuno-
globulin was bound to the patient or the control brain in vivo,
sections were also stained using only the peroxidase-conjugated
rabbit anti-human antibodies. Immunofluorescence double stain-
ing was performed with anti-amphiphysin antiserum, the micro-
glial marker KP1 (DAKO), the pan-neuronal marker PGP 9.5
(Ultraclone, Wellow, UK), and anti-human IgG using Cy2 and Cy3
(Dianova, Hamburg, Germany) as fluorochromes.
Results. Autopsy findings. The most severe histologic
abnormalities were seen in the pons and spinal cord with
marked diffuse and partly nodular lymphocytic infiltrates
and perivascular lymphocytic cuffs (figure 2, a and b). There
was marked loss of neurons in pontine nuclei and intense
gliosis in the gray matter. The inflammatory infiltrates con-
sisted predominantly of CD8-positive T-lymphocytes with

fewer CD4-positive T-cells and rare CD20-positive
B-lymphocytes (figure 2, c, e, and f). Numerous microglial
cells were seen in areas of lymphocytic infiltrates. In the
dorsal aspect of the pons, the ramified type of microglia pre-
dominated (figure 2d). Minor perivascular lymphocytic cuffs
and nodular lymphocytic infiltrates were seen in the hip-
pocampus. The terminal complement component C5b9 was
present in vessel walls and in the inflammatory infiltrates
(data not shown).
Binding studies. The patient’s plasma filtrate bound
to laminae I and II of the dorsal horn (figure 3a) and to
presynaptic structures around motor neurons (figure 3b) in
rat spinal cord in dilutions of up to 1:50,000 whereas rat
brainstem and cerebellum were negative. Similar staining
patterns were seen with anti-GAD patient serum and with
anti-GAD and anti-amphiphysin antiserum (figure 3c). Se-
rum from all other controls did not stain rat tissue (figure
3d). Preincubation with the patient’ s plasma filtrate
blocked the specific anti-amphiphysin staining completely,
indicating that the patient’s plasma filtrate in fact bound
to amphiphysin on the tissue (data not shown).
On the patient and the autopsy control tissue, the pa-
tient’s plasma filtrate bound to the dorsal horn of the spi-
nal cord and to cellular structures in the pons. Commercial
anti-GAD- and anti-amphiphysin-antisera showed similar
staining patterns. None of the control sera stained brain
structures other than blood vessel walls. Reacting the pa-
tient’s brain with antibodies to human IgG produced a
diffuse staining pattern (figure 3e), indicating that circu-
lating anti-amphiphysin antibodies had had access to CNS
parenchyma intra vitam. Owing to postmortem alterations
it was not possible to discern subcellular structures. In the
control brain, only vessel walls were faintly stained (figure
3f). Immunofluorescence double staining revealed that
neurons (figure 3g) and microglial cells in the patient’s
brain were immunoreactive for human IgG (figure 3h).
